unit.title: Perform weld in flat and horizontal positions using flux cored arc welding process (FCAW)

summary: This unit teaches you to weld mild steel plate in the flat and horizontal positions with flux-cored arc welding (FCAW), a wire-feed process that is fast, gives good penetration and, with self-shielded wire, works outdoors. You will learn to control its heavy fume, choose and store the wire, set the polarity, drive rolls, voltage, wire speed and stick-out, and make multi-pass fillet welds and a single-V butt weld on a backing strip. You will also learn to clean between passes, inspect the welds, find faults and report them.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). **Flux-cored arc welding (FCAW)** uses a continuous **tubular wire** with **flux inside it**, fed from a spool through a gun. The arc melts the wire and the plate; the flux protects the weld pool and leaves a layer of **slag** on the bead, like a stick electrode. Some wires also need a shielding gas; others make all their own shielding.

FCAW lays down weld metal much faster than stick welding, because you do not stop to change electrodes, and it penetrates well on thicker plate. Self-shielded wire needs no gas cylinder, so it is popular for site work in Jamaica: steel buildings, canopies, tank stands, trailers, gates and repairs in the yard. Gas-shielded wire gives a smoother finish in the workshop.

**Who it is for:** Welding Level 2 trainees who have learned safe arc welding, joint preparation and slag removal, for example in the MMAW unit. You will weld 10 mm mild steel plate in the **flat** and **horizontal** positions.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Control electric shock, arc radiation, heavy fume, spatter, fire, hot slag and wire hazards; wear the right PPE.
Read the job card, drawing and welding procedure; get the right plate, wire, gas and tools; make the area safe.
Choose and look after the wire
Read the wire's classification and label; choose self-shielded or gas-shielded; store it dry.
Set the polarity with the machine off, fit knurled drive rolls and the right tip, load and feed the wire, set the gas flow.
Set voltage, wire feed speed and stick-out from the maker's chart, and adjust them from a test bead.
Clean, bevel, fit up and tack tee joints and single-V butt joints, with a backing strip where the procedure says.
Make multi-pass fillet welds (1F, 2F) and butt welds (1G) with a drag angle, cleaning off the slag between every pass.
Remove the slag, check the welds with a fillet gauge, name faults and their causes, report them, and leave the area safe.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the process, fume, safety, polarity, wire, gas, settings, technique, positions, joint preparation, defects and inspection.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: three-pass fillet welds on tee joints in 10 mm plate in the horizontal position (2F); and a single-V butt weld in 10 mm plate in the flat position (1G) on a backing strip, inspected by the group.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms in the Revision section. Short answers ask for words such as chipping hammer, wire brush, root face, tack welds, spatter, burn-through, porosity, ozone and safety data sheet, and for what the letters in a wire's classification mean.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: FCAW has the hazards of all arc welding (shock, arc light, fire and burns), plus two that are worse than with solid-wire MIG: **much more fume** and **more spatter**. It also has the hazards of the wire itself and, with gas-shielded wire, a gas cylinder.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: The wire, contact tip and work are live while the trigger is pressed; wet skin, sweat and wet ground let current through you
Never stand in water or weld in the rain
Gun, cables and clamp checked before use
Switch off and isolate before changing polarity, rolls or tips
Ultraviolet and infrared light burn the eyes (arc eye) and skin
Screens; warn others before you strike
The burning flux makes heavy smoke: fine particles of metal oxides and flux, plus gases such as **ozone** (made when the arc's ultraviolet light acts on the air) and carbon monoxide
FCAW throws out a lot of hot spatter, which can start fires and burn skin
Anything that burns moved away or covered with a fire-resistant blanket
Slag flies off hot and sharp when it is chipped
Clear safety glasses under the helmet
Chip away from your face and other people
The wire end is sharp and comes out of the gun fast when inched; it can pierce skin or an eye. A loose spool can spring and unwind.
Never point the gun at anyone, or look into it, while feeding wire
Hold the wire end when cutting it off or loading a spool
A falling cylinder can break its valve. In a small, closed space the gas can push out the air and suffocate you.
Valve closed when not in use
Hot plate, slag and spatter; grinding and chipping noise
Gauntlets, tongs, hot work marked HOT

ul: Use **local exhaust ventilation** (an extraction hood or arm) with its mouth close to the arc, drawing the fume away from your face. Check it is switched on and working before you start.
Keep your **head to the side, out of the rising plume**. Do not lean over the work.
Weld in a ventilated booth, with screens, so others are not in the fume or the arc light.
Grind off paint, oil, zinc (galvanising) and other coatings before welding: they make far worse fume.
Where extraction cannot keep the fume down, wear the respirator your instructor gives you, and make sure it fits.
Read the **safety data sheet (SDS)** for the wire: it gives the fume hazards and the controls.

blocks.note: Breathing welding fume can cause coughing, headaches, a sore throat and **metal fume fever** (flu-like chills and fever a few hours later). Over many years it can damage the lungs and nerves. Closing the booth door to keep the smoke in, or welding faster, does not protect you; extraction does.
blocks.label: Safety

head: PPE
Why
Check
rows: Welding helmet with filter, about shade 11–13 depending on the current
Filter right for the current; not cracked
Worn under the helmet: hot slag when chipping, grit when grinding
Flame-resistant cotton or leather clothing, long sleeves
Collar and cuffs buttoned; no oil; no synthetic fabrics
Heavier spatter, especially on multi-pass work
Fume where extraction is not enough
The type the risk assessment names; fits your face

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat and rain both raise the risk of shock: sweat soaks gloves, and site work after rain means wet ground. Keep spare dry gloves, stand on a dry board or mat, and never weld standing in water. A sheet of steel on a wet floor makes things worse, not better.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The machine feeds the wire continuously through the gun when you press the trigger. Current passes into the wire at the **contact tip**, and an arc burns between the wire and the plate. The wire melts into the weld pool. The flux in the core makes gases that shield the pool, cleans and alloys the weld metal, and forms a **slag** that covers the hot bead. A gas-shielded wire also has shielding gas flowing through the nozzle.

head: Point
Self-shielded flux-cored wire
Gas-shielded flux-cored wire
rows: All from the flux in the wire: **no gas cylinder**
From the flux **plus** a shielding gas: carbon dioxide, or an argon and carbon dioxide mix
**Many run on DCEN** (some on DCEP): check the label
Site work outdoors: wind does not blow its shielding away as easily, and the kit is easy to carry
Workshop work on thicker plate: smoother arc, less spatter, good penetration, neater bead
More fume and spatter; rougher-looking bead
Needs a gas cylinder; must be screened from draughts

blocks.p: Both kinds leave slag that must be removed, and both need good fume control.

head: Compared with
Advantages of FCAW
Disadvantages of FCAW
rows: No stopping to change electrodes, so fewer stops and starts
Faster, with more weld metal laid per hour
Machine and wire feeder cost more
Gun and cables heavier to move about
More weld metal laid faster, with good penetration on thicker plate
Copes better with light mill scale
Slag to remove after every pass

head: Part
Its job
Check before use
rows: A **constant-voltage** DC machine: you set the voltage, and the current follows the wire feed speed
Holds the spool and drives the wire with **drive rolls**
Knurled rolls of the right size fitted
Spool brake set so the spool does not overrun
Where the gun lead and work lead are connected to + and −
Set for the wire, connections tight
Carries the wire, current (and gas) to the gun
Tip size matches the wire; hole not worn oval or blocked
Nozzle clear of spatter (or a gasless shroud for self-shielded wire)
Clamp on clean metal close to the weld
For gas-shielded wire: sets the gas flow
Cylinder chained; no leaks; flow set

blocks.note: Any damage to the gun cable, work lead or plug means **stop**. Switch off, tag the equipment DO NOT USE and report it. Never tape over a cut in a cable and carry on.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Flux-cored wires for mild steel are usually marked with an American (AWS) classification such as **E71T-1C**. Some also carry an ISO code; your instructor will show you how to read it.

head: Part of E71T-1C
What it tells you
rows: **Electrode**: the wire carries the current and melts into the weld
Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal: 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa)
Welding positions: **1 = all positions**; **0 = flat and horizontal only**
**Tubular**: a hollow wire with flux inside
The wire's type and how it is used, which also fixes its shielding and polarity. -1 is a gas-shielded type that runs on DCEP
The shielding gas it is made for: **C = carbon dioxide (CO2)**; **M = mixed gas**, mostly **argon** (often about 75–80% argon, the rest CO2)

head: Example wire
Shielding
Usual polarity
Notes
rows: General multi-pass work on thinner plate
Single-pass work on thin steel; common on small machines

blocks.note: The label or data sheet always has the last word. It gives the polarity, the gas (if any), the voltage and wire speed ranges and the stick-out for that wire. Read it before you set up.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Common sizes are 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.2 and 1.6 mm. Thicker wire carries more current and lays more metal; 1.2 mm is a common size for 10 mm plate in the workshop. The contact tip and drive rolls must match the wire size.

ul: **Carbon dioxide (CO2)**: low cost, deep penetration, a little more spatter.
**Argon and CO2 mix**: smoother arc, less spatter, neater bead. Argon makes up most of the mix.

Use the gas the wire is classified for (C or M), at the flow the procedure gives, often about 15–20 litres per minute. Too little lets air in; too much makes the gas swirl and pull air in. Neither cures a draught: screen it.
Oxygen and acetylene, natural gas and helium are **not** used for flux-cored welding of mild steel.

blocks.p: The flux inside the wire can **take in moisture** from the air, and Jamaica's warm, humid weather makes this worse, especially near the sea and in the rainy seasons. Damp flux gives **porosity**, **worm tracks** and hydrogen in the weld, which can lead to cracking. Rust or dirt on the wire also causes porosity and poor feeding.

ul: Keep new spools **sealed in their original bags and boxes** until needed, in a clean, dry store room, off the floor and away from water, steam and sea air.
Keep the label with the spool so the wire type and batch are known.
When a spool is on the machine, keep the feeder cover closed. If it will not be used for a few days or more, take it off and seal it back in its bag, as the maker advises.
Handle spools carefully: a dented spool or crushed wire will not feed smoothly.
Use the oldest stock first.
Do not use wire that is rusty or wet: set it aside and report it to your instructor.

flow: Read the job card, drawing and procedure: wire type and size, plate thickness, joint and position
Read the wire label: self-shielded or gas-shielded, polarity, gas, voltage, wire speed and stick-out
**Switch the machine off and isolate it**
Set the polarity: connect the gun lead and work lead to the right terminals and tighten them
Fit **knurled drive rolls** of the right size
Load the spool so it unwinds the right way; hold the wire end so it cannot spring loose; cut off any bent end
Feed the wire into the inlet guide and over the rolls; close the pressure arm and set the tension
Take the nozzle and contact tip off, keep the gun cable straight, and inch the wire through, with the gun pointed away from everyone
Fit the contact tip that matches the wire size, and the nozzle or gasless shroud
For gas-shielded wire, fit the regulator, open the cylinder and set the flow
Fix the work clamp on clean metal close to the weld
Set the voltage and wire feed speed from the maker's chart, and make a test bead on scrap of the same thickness

blocks.p: **Polarity** is the way the gun lead and the work lead are connected to the **positive (+)** and **negative (−)** terminals of the DC machine. On many small machines you change it by swapping the two short leads on the polarity terminals inside the wire feed compartment.

Wrong polarity gives an **unstable arc, heavy spatter, poor penetration** and often porosity. If a wire that normally runs well suddenly spatters badly after someone else has used the machine, check the polarity first.

ul: Flux-cored wire is **hollow**, so it is softer than solid wire. Use **knurled** (toothed) V-groove rolls, which grip it without squeezing it flat.
Smooth V-groove rolls are for solid steel wire; U-groove rolls are for soft aluminium wire.
Set the roll pressure **just enough** to feed the wire steadily. Too tight crushes the wire, flux spills into the liner and feeding becomes rough. Too loose and the rolls slip.
A quick check: with the gun held a little way from an insulated surface, the wire should feed smoothly; if the tip is blocked, the rolls should slip rather than the wire crumple.

blocks.h: The settings and what they do

head: Setting
What it controls
Too high
Too low
rows: The **current** (amps) and so the heat and the amount of metal laid
Bigger bead, more heat, risk of burn-through on thin parts
Long arc, wide flat bead, more spatter, undercut; with self-shielded wire, a greater risk of porosity
Wire **stubs** into the plate; rough, jerky arc; tall, narrow, humped bead
How far the wire sticks out past the tip. Flux-cored wire usually needs a **longer** stick-out than solid wire, as the maker states
Current drops; poor penetration; arc wanders; porosity with some wires
Spatter builds up on the tip and nozzle; the tip overheats; wire can burn back to the tip
How much metal goes into each part of the joint
Narrow, thin bead; undercut; poor fusion
Heavy, humped bead; overlap; slag runs ahead
Swirling gas pulls in air: porosity

blocks.note: Typical figures only, from makers' charts: many gas-shielded wires use a stick-out of about 15–25 mm, while self-shielded wires range from about 15 mm to over 50 mm; solid-wire MIG uses about 6–12 mm. A 1.2 mm gas-shielded wire on 10 mm plate in the flat position is often run somewhere around 22–28 V. **Always set up from the label or data sheet for your wire, then fine-tune from a test bead**, as your instructor shows you.
blocks.label: Remember

head: What you see and hear
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Wire stubs and pushes the gun back; rough arc; tall narrow bead
Voltage too low for the wire speed
Long, hissing arc; wide flat bead; heavy spatter; undercut
Thin bead that sits on top; poor fusion at the toes
Wire speed (current) too low, or travel too fast
Raise the wire speed, or slow down
Smooth, steady arc; slag peels well; bead flat to slightly convex, blending into the plate
Keep the settings; check them again on the job

head: Problem
Common causes
What to do
rows: Worn or blocked liner or tip
Stop, switch off, find the cause, or report it. Never pull wire through the gun by hand with the trigger pressed.
Bird's nest (wire tangled at the rolls)
Wire blocked at the tip or in the liner while the rolls keep pushing
Tip too small for the wire
Switch off, cut out the tangle, find the blockage, refeed
Switch off, change the tip, check the feed
Change the tip; tighten connections; clean the clamp position

blocks.note: Change the contact tip when its hole is worn oval or blocked with spatter. A worn tip gives a wandering, erratic arc.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Code
Weld
Position
rows: Flat: the weld lies in a trough, with the face horizontal, welded from above
Horizontal: for example a tee joint with one plate flat on the bench and the other upright, welded in the corner
Flat: plates lying flat, welded from above
Horizontal: plates upright, the joint running across

blocks.p: A wire with **0** after the 7 (such as E70T-1C) is made for flat and horizontal welding only. A wire with **1** (E71T-...) can also be used in the vertical and overhead positions.

ul: **Tee joint:** one plate stands upright on the face of the other, like the letter T; welded with a fillet weld on one or both sides.
**Lap joint:** one plate overlaps the other; fillet welded along the edge.
**Corner joint:** two edges meet at an angle, making an L.
**Butt joint:** edges meet in the same plane. Thick plate is bevelled so the weld reaches the full thickness.

flow: Cut the plate to size and remove burrs
Grind off rust, heavy mill scale, paint, oil and zinc for about 25 mm back from the joint, on both sides where the weld will be
For a butt joint, bevel each edge with the grinder to the angle the procedure gives (often about 30° each, a 60° included angle), checking with a bevel gauge
Leave or grind the **root face** (the small flat at the bottom of the bevel) as the procedure says
Fit up the parts square and in line, with the gap the procedure gives
Tack them firmly so they cannot move; chip the slag off the tacks

blocks.note: The flux can cope with a little light scale, but heavy mill scale and rust still cause **porosity and poor fusion**. Clean to bright metal.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Single-V butt joint on a backing strip

blocks.p: A **backing strip** is a strip of steel tacked under the joint. The root pass fuses into it, so the root is fully penetrated and supported, and the strip normally stays on as part of the joint. With a backing strip, the root gap is usually wider than for an open root (often about 5–6 mm), so the arc can reach down and fuse both bevels into the strip. The procedure gives the gap.

flow: Bevel both plates and check the angle
Clean the plates and the backing strip to bright metal; the strip must sit tight against the underside with no gap
Set the root gap evenly along the joint
Tack the plates to the backing strip, outside the weld area or at the ends, and check they are in line
Weld the root pass, fusing into both bevels and the strip; then fill and cap passes, cleaning off all the slag between every pass

ul: Tack well, with tacks at both ends and at even spacing along long joints.
On long joints, weld short runs in a balanced order (or back-step) rather than one long hot pass.
Clamp the work where you can, and pre-set the parts slightly against the pull of the weld.
Do not over-weld: extra weld metal means extra shrinking.
Let welds cool in air. Never cool them with water or a wet rag: it can crack the weld.

blocks.p: Flux-cored welding normally uses the **drag** (pull) technique: the gun points **back** at the finished weld, and you pull it along the joint. A drag angle of about 10–20° from upright is usual. Dragging keeps the slag **behind** the pool. If you push the gun, the slag runs ahead of the pool and is trapped under the weld (**slag inclusion**). Many welders remember: "If there's slag, you drag."

ul: Keep the arc on the **leading edge** of the pool, so it melts into fresh plate and does not ride on top of the molten metal.
Hold the stick-out steady at the length the maker gives. A wandering stick-out changes the current.
Travel at a steady speed that keeps the bead the same width.
Watch the pool, not the bright arc: you should see the pool melting into both sides of the joint.

head: Weld
Work angle (seen from the end)
Travel angle
rows: About 90° to the plate, centred on the joint
About **45°**, aimed **into the root**, slightly towards the bottom plate
Tilted to aim each pass at the toe it must cover (see below)

blocks.h: Three-pass horizontal fillet (2F) on a tee joint

flow: Clean the plates, tack the upright plate square on the base plate, set up from the chart and test on scrap
**Pass 1 (root):** aim into the root at about 45°, slightly towards the bottom plate, with a steady drag angle and stick-out; fuse into both plates
Chip off **all** the slag and wire brush the bead, wearing safety glasses
**Pass 2:** lay it along the **bottom plate**, aimed at the lower toe of pass 1, covering about half of it
Clean off all the slag again
**Pass 3:** lay it along the **upright plate**, aimed at the upper toe of pass 2, filling the rest of the joint and blending into the upright plate without undercut
Fill the crater at the end of every pass; remove all the slag; check the legs with a fillet gauge

blocks.note: In the horizontal fillet position gravity pulls the molten metal down onto the bottom plate. That gives a long bottom leg, a short top leg, **undercut on the upright plate** and **overlap on the bottom plate**. Aim slightly higher on the later passes, keep the voltage and travel speed right, and do not weave wide.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Single-V butt weld in the flat position (1G)

ul: **Root pass:** centred in the joint, fusing into both bevels and the backing strip. Watch both sides melt in.
**Fill passes:** stringer beads, or a slight weave, placed to fill the groove evenly; each pass fused into the bevel faces and the pass below.
**Cap pass:** fills the joint just above the plate surface, even in width and height, blending into the plate at both edges without undercut.
Keep the slag off: clean every pass completely before the next. Grind out any slag trapped at the sides of a pass.
Start with the wire at the right stick-out; strike on the joint, not on the plate beside it.
At the end of a pass, **pause briefly to fill the crater** before you release the trigger. An unfilled crater can crack.
After releasing the trigger, keep the gun in place for a moment if gas is used, so the gas still covers the cooling crater.
To restart, clean the slag off the end of the bead, strike just ahead of the crater, move back into it, then carry on.
Let the slag darken, then chip it off with a **chipping hammer**, striking away from your face, and clean the bead and toes with a **wire brush**.
Wear safety glasses under the helmet: hot slag flies.
Look closely at the toes of the bead, where slag hides. Grind out any slag that will not come off, and any sharp hump that the next pass could trap slag under.
Never pour water on the weld to crack the slag off.

head: Fault
What it looks like
Main causes
How to prevent it
rows: Slag trapped in the weld or between passes
Slag not fully removed between passes
Pushing the gun so slag runs ahead
Weave too wide; travel too slow
Chip and brush every pass; grind out slag pockets
Round gas holes; or long, worm-shaped gas marks on the surface of the bead
Gas flow wrong or blown away by a draught; nozzle blocked with spatter
Stick-out and settings from the label
Correct gas flow; screen draughts; clean the nozzle
Weld metal not melted into the plate or the pass below
Too little heat (wire speed too low)
Travel too fast or too slow
Arc riding on top of the pool
Arc on the leading edge of the pool
The root has not fused through, or into the backing strip
Gap too small or root face too big
A groove melted along the toe and left unfilled; on 2F, usually on the **upright plate**
Aim to fill the upper toe
Weld metal rolled onto the bottom plate without fusing to it
One fillet leg longer than the other
Bead stands high with sharp toes
Many balls of metal stuck round the weld
A hole melted right through the root
Lines in or beside the weld, or star-shaped in a crater
Correct weld size; cool in air
Burnt spots on the plate beside the weld
Striking outside the joint; gun touching the job

blocks.note: **Cracks** are the most serious fault. Show any crack to your instructor; it is ground out completely and re-welded.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: When you find a fault, name it, give its likely cause, and say what you will change. That is what the assessor wants to hear.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Remove all the slag with a chipping hammer, wearing safety glasses, then wire brush the weld
In good light, check the bead: even width and ripple, smooth blending into both plates at the toes
Check the size with a **fillet weld gauge**: legs equal and the size on the drawing; the face not too thin or too humped
Look for undercut, overlap, porosity or worm tracks, slag in the ripples, cracks, unfilled craters, arc strikes and heavy spatter; check the starts and stops closely
On a butt weld, check the cap height and width, and the root fused into the backing strip along its length
Check the parts are still square and in line
Record the results on the inspection sheet

head: Good fillet weld
Poor fillet weld
rows: Equal legs of the right size
Smooth toes, no undercut or overlap
Even ripples, no holes, no slag left
Tall, narrow bead with sharp toes
Groove on the upright plate; metal rolled onto the bottom plate
Slag in the ripples; worm marks; heavy spatter

ul: Mark it with chalk or soapstone.
Write it on the inspection sheet with the job number.
Tell your instructor. Do **not** hide it with grinding or paint.
The instructor decides whether it can be repaired (for example ground out and re-welded) or whether the job must be done again.

flow: Release the trigger, finish the crater and hang the gun up where it cannot touch the work
For gas-shielded wire: close the cylinder valve and release the gas from the line as the instructor shows
Switch the machine off and isolate it
Close the wire feeder cover, or bag and seal the spool if it will not be used for some days
Coil the gun cable and work lead loosely and hang them up
Leave hot work to cool in a safe place, marked HOT
Sweep up slag, wire offcuts and stubs and put them in the **metal scrap bin**, never in a paper bin with rags
Check the area for anything smouldering; return tools and PPE

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Cut gun cable, damaged work clamp or plug, a machine that trips or smells of burning
Stop, switch off, tag it DO NOT USE, report it
Wire that keeps stopping, a worn liner, damaged rolls
Stop and switch off; report it rather than forcing the wire
Rusty or damp wire, wire running low, gas cylinder nearly empty
Report so stock is replaced or reordered
Burns, arc eye, slag in the eye, a shock or tingle, a small fire
Get first aid; make sure it is recorded
Faults found, results of checks, job finished

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain how FCAW works and compare self-shielded and gas-shielded wire.
I can say why FCAW makes more fume than solid-wire MIG and how to control it.
I can name the hazards of FCAW and choose the right PPE, including the filter shade.
I can read a classification such as E71T-1C and say what each part means.
I can store and handle flux-cored wire so it stays dry and feeds well.
I can set the polarity safely for the wire, fit knurled drive rolls and the right tip, and feed the wire through.
I can explain what wire feed speed, voltage and stick-out each do, and adjust them from a test bead.
I can name the positions 1F, 2F, 1G and 2G.
I can clean, bevel, fit up and tack tee joints and single-V butt joints, with a backing strip.
I can weld with a drag angle, keeping the arc on the leading edge of the pool.
I can make a three-pass horizontal fillet weld and a multi-pass flat butt weld, cleaning off all the slag between passes.
I can inspect a weld with a fillet gauge, name FCAW faults with their causes and cures, and report faults.
I can shut down, store the wire and leave the area safe.

terms: A steel strip under a butt joint that the root pass fuses into
Wire tangled at the drive rolls because it cannot feed forward
A hole melted right through the plate by too much heat
The hammer used to chip slag off a weld
The copper tip in the gun that passes current into the wire
DC electrode negative and DC electrode positive: the two polarities
Pointing the gun back at the finished weld and pulling it along
The rolls in the wire feeder that push the wire; knurled for flux-cored wire
The first letter of a wire's classification: the wire is the electrode
A gauge that checks the leg length and shape of a fillet weld
Flux-cored wire used with a shielding gas, usually on DCEP
A harmful gas with a sharp smell, made when the arc's ultraviolet light acts on the air
Which DC terminal (+ or −) the gun lead is connected to
Gas holes trapped in the weld metal
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevelled edge
The maker's sheet giving the hazards and controls for the wire
Flux-cored wire that needs no gas; many run on DCEN
The crust formed from the flux that covers the hot weld
Small balls of metal thrown out by the arc that stick to the plate
The length of wire between the contact tip and the arc
Short welds that hold the parts in place before the full weld
One plate standing upright on another, like the letter T
A hollow wire with flux inside
The brush used to clean a weld after the slag is chipped off
How fast the wire is fed; it sets the welding current
Long, worm-shaped gas marks on the surface of a flux-cored weld
Flat fillet, horizontal fillet, flat groove (butt) and horizontal groove positions

c1.title: A canopy frame on site in Yallahs
c1.text: Ricardo is welding the steel frame of a shop canopy on site in Yallahs, St Thomas, with a small wire-feed machine and self-shielded flux-cored wire. The wire label says "DCEN". The machine was last used in the workshop with gas-shielded wire on DCEP, and nobody has changed the leads. His first welds spatter heavily and the arc is unstable. A light breeze is blowing along the street.

c2.title: Loading a new spool in Ewarton
c2.text: At a training centre in Ewarton, St Catherine, Kayla is loading a new spool of 1.2 mm gas-shielded flux-cored wire. The machine still has the 1.0 mm contact tip from the last job. The label gives a stick-out of 20–25 mm, but Kayla is used to solid-wire MIG and keeps the stick-out at about 8 mm. After a few minutes the wire tangles into a bird's nest at the drive rolls.

c3.title: Trailer brackets in Junction
c3.text: Leroy works at a trailer shop in Junction, St Elizabeth, making three-pass horizontal (2F) fillet welds on 12 mm brackets with gas-shielded flux-cored wire. The drawing asks for 10 mm legs. On the first bracket his fillet gauge shows a 12 mm leg on the bottom plate and an 8 mm leg on the upright plate. Small pockets of slag are left at the toes of his root pass, and his last pass stands high and humped with sharp toes.

c4.title: A draughty bay in Discovery Bay
c4.text: A small shop in Discovery Bay, St Ann, uses gas-shielded flux-cored wire with CO2. The roller door of the welding bay faces the sea and is usually left open for air. Welds made near the door show worm tracks and pinholes. The gas nozzle is half blocked with spatter, and the flowmeter has been turned up to 40 litres per minute "to beat the breeze".

c5.title: A butt weld on a backing strip in Highgate
c5.text: At a training centre in Highgate, St Mary, a group is welding a single-V butt joint in 10 mm plate in the flat position (1G) on a steel backing strip. Each plate is bevelled to 30°. After the root pass, the underside shows a clear line where the backing strip has not fused to one plate. Later, the cap shows a short length of undercut, and one trainee suggests grinding the cap flat "so the assessor won't see it".

questions.q: How should the leads be connected for Ricardo's wire?
o: Gun lead to positive (+), work lead to negative (−)
Gun lead to negative (−), work lead to positive (+)
Both leads to the negative (−) terminal
Either way, as self-shielded wire is not affected
questions.why: DCEN means the electrode (the gun and wire) is negative: gun lead to −, work lead to +. Switch off and isolate the machine before swapping the leads, and tighten them firmly.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the heavy spatter and unstable arc?
o: The breeze blowing the arc to one side
Wire that is too new and still too dry
The leads left set for DCEP from before
A work lead that is too short for site work
questions.why: The wire needs DCEN, but the machine was left on DCEP. Wrong polarity gives an unstable arc, heavy spatter, poor penetration and often porosity.

questions.q: Ricardo is working outdoors. What should he still do about the fume?
o: Nothing, as fume is not a problem in the open air
Wear a paper dust mask over his nose and carry on
Lean in close so the breeze cannot reach the arc
Stand so the breeze takes the plume away from him
questions.why: Self-shielded wire makes heavy fume. Outdoors, position yourself so the breeze takes the plume away and keep your head out of it; use a respirator if your instructor says.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the bird's nest?
o: The 1.0 mm tip is too small for 1.2 mm wire
The spool is too new and the wire too springy
The gas flow is set too low for the wire size
The work clamp is fixed too far from the weld
questions.why: A tip that is too small for the wire grips it, so the wire cannot move forward while the rolls keep pushing, and it tangles at the rolls. Fit the tip that matches the wire size.

questions.q: How should Kayla feed the new wire through the gun?
o: Tip fitted, gun pointed at the plate so she can watch
Pulled through by hand with the trigger held on
Cable coiled tightly so the wire takes the bends
Tip off, cable straight, gun aimed away from people
questions.why: Taking the tip off and keeping the cable straight lets the wire feed freely. The wire comes out fast and sharp, so the gun is never pointed at anyone, or looked into, while inching.

questions.q: What is likely to happen if Kayla keeps holding an 8 mm stick-out with this wire?
o: The weld will cool faster and come out much stronger
The bead will be flatter, with almost no slag to remove
Spatter builds up on the tip, which overheats
The wire will feed faster than the speed she has set
questions.why: Flux-cored wire is made to run at a longer stick-out than solid wire. Too short a stick-out puts the tip close to the arc: spatter builds up on it, it overheats, and the wire can burn back to it.

questions.q: Leroy's bottom leg is 12 mm and his top leg 8 mm. What should he change on the next bracket?
o: Aim the later passes higher, onto the upright plate
Push the gun instead of dragging it, to lift the metal upward
Turn the voltage up as high as it goes for the last pass
Weave the root pass wide enough to reach both legs at once
questions.why: In 2F gravity pulls metal onto the bottom plate. Aiming the second pass at the lower toe and the third at the upper toe, as the pass sequence says, builds the upright leg up to size.

questions.q: What should Leroy do about the slag pockets at the toes of the root pass?
o: Weld straight over them, as the next pass melts the slag
Leave them, since slag at the toes is not a fault
Chip and brush, then grind out any slag that stays
Pour water on the weld so the slag cracks off cleanly
questions.why: Slag left at the toes is trapped by the next pass as a slag inclusion. Chip and brush every pass, and grind out pockets that will not come off; never quench the weld.

questions.q: The last pass stands high and humped, with sharp toes. What are the likely causes?
o: Voltage too high and travel much too fast
Voltage too low, or travel too slow
Wire too dry and drive rolls too loose
Gas flow too low and stick-out too long
questions.why: A low voltage gives a short arc and a tall, narrow, humped bead that does not wet out at the toes, and slow travel piles the metal up. Raise the voltage a little and keep a steady speed.

questions.q: Where should Leroy lay the second of his three passes?
o: Along the upright plate, aimed at the upper toe of the root
Straight on top of the root pass, centred on it
Anywhere, as long as all the slag has been removed first
Along the bottom plate, over about half the root pass
questions.why: The second pass goes along the bottom plate, aimed at the lower toe of the root pass; the third pass then goes along the upright plate. This builds equal legs without overlap or undercut.

questions.q: What is the main cause of the worm tracks in welds made near the door?
o: The sea breeze blowing away the shielding gas
The CO2 gas being too pure for this wire
The plates being cleaned too well before welding
The welders using the drag technique
questions.why: A draught blows the shielding gas away from the pool, so air gets in and leaves porosity and worm tracks. Screen the bay or close the door, and keep good fume extraction.

questions.q: What should be done about the 40 L/min gas flow?
o: Raise it further to 60 L/min, since the breeze still gets through
Turn the gas off and weld with the gas-shielded wire alone
Leave it, as more gas can only make the shielding better
Set it back to the procedure's flow and screen the draught
questions.why: Too much gas swirls and pulls air into the shield, so it does not cure a draught. Set the flow the procedure gives (often about 15–20 L/min) and stop the draught with screens.

questions.q: Why does the half-blocked nozzle matter?
o: It upsets the gas, so the pool is poorly shielded
Spatter in the nozzle makes the wire feed faster
It makes the contact tip the wrong size for the wire
It changes the machine's polarity to DCEN
questions.why: Spatter in the nozzle disturbs the gas, letting air reach the pool and cause porosity. Clean the nozzle regularly, and change the tip when it is worn or blocked.

questions.q: Why has the root pass not fused into the backing strip under one plate?
o: The backing strip was cleaned to bright metal first
The 30° bevels made the groove much too wide to fuse
The wire was aimed to one side, or heat was too low
The cap pass was laid before the slag had cooled
questions.why: The root pass must fuse into both bevels and the strip. Aiming to one side, too little wire speed, or too narrow a gap leaves one side unfused; a strip that is not tight against the plates makes it worse.

questions.q: Each plate is bevelled to 30°. What is the included angle of the joint?
questions.why: The included angle is the total angle between the two bevelled faces: 30° + 30° = 60°.

questions.q: What should the group do about the undercut on the cap?
o: Grind the cap flat so the undercut cannot be seen
Paint over it once the plate has cooled
Mark it, record it and tell the instructor
Leave it, as undercut on a cap does not count
questions.why: Faults are marked, recorded and reported, never hidden. The instructor decides whether it can be repaired, for example by grinding and adding weld metal, or whether the joint must be redone.

questions.q: A wire is classified E71T-11. What does the 1 straight after the 7 tell you?
o: It can be used in all positions
It is for flat and horizontal work only
It needs a single shielding gas
It must only be used for one pass
questions.why: In the classification, the digit after the strength figure gives the positions: 1 means all positions and 0 means flat and horizontal only. The -11 after the T shows the wire type: here a self-shielded wire usually run on DCEN.

questions.q: On a test bead the wire keeps stubbing into the plate and pushing the gun back, and the arc is rough. What should be changed first?
o: Lower the voltage a little
Raise the voltage a little
Swap the gas to pure argon
Change to smooth drive rolls
questions.why: Stubbing, a rough arc and a tall narrow bead mean the voltage is too low for the wire speed: the arc is too short. Raise the voltage a step and test again.

questions.q: Jodi-Ann is flux-cored welding at about 200 A. Which filter shade would a standard chart suggest?
o: Shade 5
Shade 12
Shade 8
Shade 3
questions.why: Charts give about shade 11–13 for wire-feed arc welding at this sort of current, darker for higher currents. Shades 3 to 8 are for gas welding, brazing and cutting and do not protect against an electric arc.

questions.q: Compared with stick welding (MMAW), why is FCAW faster on a long weld?
o: Its slag never needs removing between the passes
The wire is fed from a spool, so no electrode changes
It runs on a much lower current than stick welding
It needs no joint preparation or cleaning first at all
questions.why: The wire is fed continuously from a spool, so the welder does not stop every few minutes to fit a new electrode, and more weld metal is laid each hour. FCAW still leaves slag to remove.
